title: Testing two execution algorithms
objectives: Design and analyse a randomised test of two execution algorithms.

screens.title: Two orders, one stock-day
screens.prose: The experiment of lesson 8 ran for 200 stock-days. In each, a coin sent one parent order to algorithm A and one to B. Each dot is one stock-day: A's shortfall across, B's up. Lower is better.
screens.question: What does the tight diagonal cloud tell us?

options.text: Most of an order's shortfall comes from its stock-day, shared by both algorithms
The two algorithms are the same
options.why: The cloud says A and B move together, not that they are equal. The question is the small offset from the line.

options.text: B is far better than A
options.why: The dots sit close to the dashed line B = A. Any gain is small next to the spread.
Correlation between the pair is expected: both orders share the stock and the day.

hints.text: Look at how far the cloud spreads along the line and across it.
Along the line the spread is about 9 bps; across it much less.
The correlation is 0.808: the stock-day dominates.

feedback.correct: The stock-day dominates: the correlation is 0.808.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the spread along the line with the spread across it.

explain.text: The pair correlates at 0.808. Shortfall varies with the stock-day by about 8 bps, while the algorithms differ by about 1. A paired analysis removes the shared part.

screens.title: The unpaired view
screens.prose: Treat the 400 orders as two independent samples. Welch's statistic is $t = (\bar y_B - \bar y_A)/\sqrt{s_A^2/n + s_B^2/n}$.
screens.question: What is Welch's $t$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the difference in means by $\sqrt{s_A^2/200 + s_B^2/200}$.

byKey.sign: Keep the sign: B minus A is negative.
byKey.pooln: You divided by 400 in each variance. Each arm has 200 orders.
byKey.paired: That is the paired $t$. Here the orders are treated as unrelated.

explain.text: Welch's $t = -1.222$ and $p = 0.222$. The stock-day noise, about 8 bps per order, is in both variances and swamps a 1 bp effect.

screens.title: The paired view
screens.prose: Now use each stock-day's difference $D = B - A$, as `testing` lesson 8 did for pairs: $t = \bar d/(s_d/\sqrt n)$ on $n - 1$ df.
screens.question: What is the paired $t$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide $\bar d$ by $s_d/\sqrt{200}$.

byKey.welch: That is the unpaired statistic. Use the differences' SD, 5.5334.
byKey.nosqrt: You divided by $s_d$ alone. The standard error is $s_d/\sqrt{200}$.
byKey.sign: D = B − A has a negative mean, so t is negative. A positive 2.7895 drops the minus sign and reverses the direction of the effect.

explain.text: Paired, $t = -2.790$ and $p = 0.00579$, against $p = 0.222$ unpaired. The same 400 orders; the difference is in the analysis. `scipy.stats.ttest_rel` agrees.

screens.title: An interval for the gain
screens.question: What is the lower end of the interval, in bps?

feedback.correct: $(-1.8630, -0.3199)$ bps: B saves between 0.3 and 1.9 bps.

byKey.z: You used 1.96. With 199 df the multiplier is 1.9720; the gap is small but real.
byKey.sign: The mean difference is negative, so the whole interval lies below zero. A positive 1.863 drops the minus sign of the end point.

explain.text: The interval is $(-1.8630, -0.3199)$ bps. It excludes 0, matching $p = 0.00579$; the true gain in this simulation was 1 bp.

screens.title: Pairs as a regression
screens.prose:
The same analysis is a regression with a fixed effect for each stock-day:
$$y = \beta_0 + \beta_B\,[\text{algo} = B] + \sum_s \gamma_s[\text{block} = s] + \varepsilon$$
In statsmodels: `smf.ols('sf ~ C(algo) + C(blk)', data=long)`. Never name a column `is` or a Python variable `C`: both break the formula parser.
screens.question: The fitted $\hat\beta_B$ is $-1.0915$ with $t = -2.790$. Why is it the paired result exactly?

options.text: Each stock-day's dummy absorbs its shared level, leaving only within-day differences to estimate $\beta_B$

options.why: It is an identity: with two orders per block, OLS with block dummies reproduces the paired $t$.

options.text: OLS always gives the paired answer
options.why: Without the block dummies OLS gives the unpaired estimate with the unpaired, larger standard error.

feedback.correct: Block dummies remove the stock-day level.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what the 199 block dummies soak up.

explain.text: With a dummy per stock-day, only the A to B contrast within each day is left. That is ANOVA with two factors, and the same design logic carries to more arms.

screens.title: A check that ignores the tails
screens.prose: The noise has fat tails ($t_4$), so check without assuming normality. The **sign test** counts stock-days where B beat A: 117 of 200. Under no difference each count is Binomial(200, 0.5). The Wilcoxon signed-rank test, lesson 10, uses the sizes too.
screens.question: What is the two-sided exact $p$-value?

hints.text: Read the label of the two regions.

feedback.correct: $p = 0.0194$; the normal approximation with continuity correction gives 0.0196.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add both tails: 117 or more, and 83 or fewer.

byKey.one: That is one tail. The question asks two-sided.
byKey.norm: That is the normal approximation without the continuity correction.

explain.text: $2P(W \ge 117) = 0.0194$. The sign test uses only the direction of each difference, so one wild stock-day cannot sway it. It agrees with the paired $t$.

screens.prose: An analyst runs Welch's test on the experiment's 400 orders, gets $p = 0.222$, and writes: "the new algorithm makes no difference".

options.text: The design was paired; analysed as pairs, $p = 0.006$ and the interval excludes 0

options.why: A large $p$ is not evidence of no effect. Here it came from leaving the stock-day noise in.

options.text: The tails are fat, so no test can be trusted

With pairs, 200 gives about 80% power for 1 bp, as lesson 8 planned.

hints.text: Which analysis did the design plan?
The pairs share their stock-day noise.

feedback.correct: Analysed as designed, the gain is clear.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look at the analysis the design called for.

byKey.ok: You read a large $p$ as proof of no effect. It only says this analysis could not tell.

screens.title: Looking often, honestly
screens.prose: Wald's sequential test adds each stock-day's log-likelihood ratio and stops at a barrier: $\ln\frac{0.8}{0.05} = 2.7726$ above, $\ln\frac{0.2}{0.95} = -1.5581$ below. In units where $\delta/\sigma = 0.25$, each step has mean $\mp 0.03125$ and SD 0.25.

derive.caption: {{values.hitsUp}} of 300 tests stop at the top, {{values.hitsDown}} at the bottom; mean stop {{fixed(values.tauMean, 1)}} stock-days.

screens.question: Wald's approximation for the average stopping time under no effect is $\frac{0.95 \times (-1.5581) + 0.05 \times 2.7726}{-0.03125}$. What is it?

feedback.correct: About 43 stock-days under no effect and 61 under the effect. A fixed one-sided test needs 99.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the weighted barrier sum by $-0.03125$.

byKey.effect: That is the average under the effect: $(0.2 \times (-1.5581) + 0.8 \times 2.7726)/0.03125$.
byKey.fixed: That is the fixed-sample size for the same error rates.

explain.text: Wald gives 42.9 and 61.0; overshoot makes real tests run a little longer, about 48 and 68. Of these 300 seeded tests, 14 stop at the top under no effect and 246 under the effect. That is 4.7% and 82.0%, close to the planned 5% and 80%.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats


def analyse_paired(a, b):
    d = np.asarray(b, dtype=float) - np.asarray(a, dtype=float)
    n = len(d)
    se = d.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)
    t = d.mean() / se
    p = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), n - 1)
    q = stats.t.ppf(0.975, n - 1)
    return d.mean(), t, p, d.mean() - q * se, d.mean() + q * se


def sign_test(a, b):
    d = np.asarray(b, dtype=float) - np.asarray(a, dtype=float)
    d = d[d != 0]
    wins = int(np.sum(d < 0))
    return wins, stats.binomtest(wins, len(d), 0.5).pvalue

screens.title: The note to the head of trading
screens.prose: The desk trades £2bn a month through these algorithms. The experiment estimates that B saves 1.0915 bps, with a 95% interval of 0.32 to 1.86 bps. One basis point is 0.01%.
screens.question: What is the estimated saving in pounds per month?

feedback.correct: About £218,000 a month, between £64,000 and £373,000 on the interval.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. One bp is $10^{-4}$ of the amount traded.

byKey.pct: You treated a bp as 1%. It is 0.01%.

explain.text: $\text{£}2\text{bn} \times 1.0915 \times 10^{-4} = \text{£}218{,}293$ a month; the interval gives £63,980 to £372,606. The note should state the design, the paired analysis, and the stopping rule fixed in advance.

ideas: Analyse a paired design as pairs: on 200 stock-days, $p = 0.00579$ paired against 0.222 unpaired.
The sign test is a check that ignores tail size: B won 117 of 200 days, $p = 0.0194$.
Peeking at a fixed-sample test inflates false alarms to 19.4% with 10 looks. A sequential test sets its barriers in advance.

quiz.prose: In a paired execution test, the B order of one stock-day was cancelled halfway.
quiz.question: How should the analysis treat that stock-day?

options.text: Drop the whole stock-day, both orders
Drop only the cancelled B order and keep the A order
options.why: A lone A order has no partner, so it gives no difference. Keeping it in an A mean brings back the stock-day noise.

options.text: Use the half-filled B order as it stands
options.why: A half-filled order's shortfall is not comparable with a complete one.

feedback.correct: The block is the unit: drop it whole.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The paired analysis works on complete pairs.

explain.text: Each stock-day contributes one difference. Without a complete pair, the block drops out, and the report should say how many were dropped and why.
